analysis.one_liner: Lets savings and loan associations hold thinner capital reserves against losses until 1997.
analysis.headline: The bill never came to a vote: after a subcommittee hearing in the House Banking Committee, it died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: After the savings and loan crisis, Congress had ordered thrifts to build capital reserves — money cushioning losses — at least as strict as the rules for national banks. This bill would have postponed those stricter rules for about five years, held the leverage requirement at a flat 3% of assets, cut the risk-based requirement to 90% of what banks face, and let the thrift regulator grant individual exemptions to qualifying institutions. Supporters said the reserves were tying up money that thrifts could lend; critics said thinner cushions shift the risk of failure onto the federal deposit insurance fund and, ultimately, taxpayers, only a few years after the S&L cleanup cost taxpayers tens of billions of dollars.
analysis.who_benefits: Savings and loan associations, especially thinly capitalized ones: they could keep more assets on their books instead of holding them as reserves, defer required capital build-ups, and in some cases win individual exemptions from the standards entirely.

how_it_helps.text: Postpones until after December 31, 1996 the requirement that thrift capital standards be no less stringent than those for national banks, and holds the leverage requirement at exactly 3% of total assets until January 1, 1997.
Sets the risk-based capital requirement for savings associations at 90% of the level applying to national banks, a 10% discount relative to banks.

Lets the Director of the Office of Thrift Supervision grant exceptions from the capital standards to institutions showing rising capital, profitability, compliance with a capital plan, no unapproved dividends, and support for community credit needs.
Sponsors and the bill's title frame the purpose as credit availability: fewer reserves tied up in capital should free money for lending, including mortgage lending.

analysis.who_pays: The federal deposit insurance fund — and taxpayers behind it — bear greater risk if thinly capitalized thrifts fail, since losses beyond reserves are covered by insurance. Savers and communities also bear the risk if weakened thrifts collapse rather than rebuild cushions.
analysis.who_pays_short: The deposit insurance fund and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Thinner capital cushions mean less protection against losses, so failures cost the deposit insurance fund more — the exact dynamic that produced the savings and loan crisis, whose cleanup taxpayers were still paying for when the bill was introduced.

The exemption authority would let individual weak thrifts delay required capital reductions until the end of 1996, extending the period during which undercapitalized institutions could keep operating.
Giving thrifts risk-based requirements 90% of banks' would keep the playing field tilted, leaving national banks at a relative disadvantage on capital.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The case for the bill rested on a real concern — capital rules can constrain lending, and 1991-92 was a period of tight credit. But the bill's answer was to postpone, discount, and waive the safety rules written after the S&L crisis for five years, and the industry asking for relief was the one whose failures had just cost taxpayers on the order of $100 billion. The burden of proof was on showing the cushion was too big, not too small, and the bill never came close to a vote.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Banking Committee, sent to its financial institutions subcommittee, had one hearing, and never got a markup or floor vote before the 102nd Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John LaFalce introduced the Credit Availability Act on February 18, 1992, with Reps. McCollum, Campbell, and Flake as original cosponsors.

The bill was referred to the Committee on Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs on the day of introduction, then to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions Supervision, Regulation and Insurance on March 3, 1992.
The subcommittee held a hearing on March 31, 1992, but no further action — no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — followed.
The bill gathered 22 cosponsors, 13 Republicans and 9 Democrats, but died in committee when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Taxpayers and the deposit insurance fund are better off the bill died, since the thrift industry did not get a five-year discount from the post-crisis capital rules. Thrifts wanting easier standards lost the chance.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers and the deposit insurance fund

for.name: Rep. John J. LaFalce
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a bipartisan cosponsor group of 22.

for.name: 13 of 22 cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsor Rep. McCollum of Florida.

against.name: House Banking Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the Committee on Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup or floor action on the bill after its subcommittee hearing.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship split 13 Republicans to 9 Democrats, and no party-line vote ever occurred because the bill died in committee.

industries.note: The bill would have let thrifts hold less loss-absorbing capital and defer required build-ups for years, freeing money for lending but shifting failure risk onto the deposit insurance fund. Just years after the S&L crisis, the industry's interest in lighter cushions ran against taxpayers who back the insurance fund.
With thrifts required to hold only 90% of banks' risk-based capital, banks would have faced a relative competitive disadvantage on capital costs. The effect on bank customers is indirect.
Thinly capitalized thrifts raise the expected cost of failures to the insurance fund and ultimately taxpayers, who were still absorbing the cost of the S&L cleanup.
